title: Muslim Artisans Weave Durga's Hair: West Bengal's Story of Harmony
excerpt: In Howrah's Parbatipur village, Muslim artisans have woven Maa Durga's wavy hair for generations — but rising jute prices and a changing social climate are fraying the trade.
body:
• Maa Durga's thick black, wavy hair — a fixture of West Bengal's Durga Puja pandals every year — is woven by Muslim artisans from Parbatipur village in Howrah's Amta locality, 50 km from Kolkata.
  • Sheikh Nawab, 37, runs the village's largest wig business, learned from his grandfather. The craft has two phases: sourcing and dyeing jute, then stitching — the longest step. A sack of wigs sells for ₹9,000–10,000 across Kumartuli, Bihar, UP, Nepal and Bangladesh.
  • The artisans face rising jute prices (₹140–150 a unit, up from ₹90), bad monsoons, strained India-Bangladesh trade, competition from machine-made Kolkata wigs, and growing reluctance from some idol makers to buy from them.
  • Diaspora hook: if your community is commissioning a Durga idol from a Kolkata maker for a US puja, ask specifically for handmade Parbatipur wigs — and see how the idols themselves come alive in our Navratri 2026 coverage.

Every year during Durga Puja, Maa Durga's thick black, wavy hair draws the eye across West Bengal's pandals. What almost no one in the crowd knows: those tresses are woven by Muslim artisans in Parbatipur, a village in Howrah district's Amta locality, about 50 kilometres from Kolkata and connected by the Baragachhia railway station.

Sheikh Nawab, 37, runs the village's largest wig business for the deity's idols. He doesn't remember which of his ancestors started the craft; he recalls learning it from his grandfather. "The crafting of wigs are done in two phases. We source the jute and dye it and then we hire several artisans to stitch them. Stitching takes the longest. We train the workers ourselves," he told The Hindu.

How the wigs are made

The work is done almost entirely by hand. Inside a small yard at Nawab's house, two thatched huts hold the operation: two of his brothers boil black dye in a large charcoal pot to colour the white jute, which then dries on a clothesline for days. In another house on the same lane, five women stitch the freshly dyed jute on sewing machines. Nawab keeps hundreds of packets of finished wigs stored in sacks; each sack sells for around ₹9,000 to ₹10,000, flowing mostly to Kumartuli — Kolkata's largest idol-making quarter — and onward to Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Nepal and Bangladesh.

https://x.com/thebetterindia/status/2109139429981896806

Falling income, rising pressure

The craft is under strain from every side. "Adverse monsoons and rising jute prices have hampered production over the last two to three years," said Sheikh Injaman, another family member. A unit of jute now costs about ₹140 to ₹150, up from ₹90 two or three years ago — a roughly 60% jump that the artisans absorb.

Trade has thinned too. Injaman said the strained relations between Bangladesh and India have hurt sales: "We had great business relations with Hindu communities in Bangladesh. But that route is proving difficult due to the deteriorating political situation. We can barely pay the hundreds of labourers from nearby villages who work for us." Meanwhile, machine-based wig-making factories in Kolkata undercut the handmade trade — artists from Kumartuli now source a good chunk of their wigs from three to five major factories instead of Parbatipur.

"Earlier, we did not hesitate to approach idol makers, particularly those from the Hindu community. But now many of them hesitate to source wigs from us."

— Shona Bibi, artisan, Parbatipur

A fragile harmony

That last pressure is the one the artisans name most quietly: a changing social climate in which communal sourcing relationships have become harder. For generations, Muslim hands have given the goddess her hair — a lived example of the syncretism that Durga Puja has long embodied. Whether the economics of the craft can survive rising input costs and factory competition will decide how much longer Parbatipur's looms keep the tradition alive.

What to watch

Diaspora puja committees that order idols from Kolkata can make a concrete choice: ask makers where the hair comes from, and whether handmade Parbatipur wigs are an option. The sacks at ₹9,000–10,000 keep an entire village's craft economy — hundreds of labourers from surrounding villages — afloat through the festival season.
